Surah 90: Al-Balad (The City)

Meccan, and its verses are twenty.

﴿Nay, I swear by this city,﴾ He, glorified is He, swore by the Sacred City (al-Balad al-Haram) and by what is joined to it, to establish that man was created as one destined to endure hardships and to suffer difficulties. He interposed between the oath and its answer with His saying, exalted is He: *

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 90, verse 2:

﴿And you are a resident of this city﴾. Either it is to honour him, peace be upon him, by making his residence therein the basis for magnifying it through the oath by it; or it is to alert from the very beginning to the certainty of the content of the response (jawab), by mentioning some of the materials of hardship, in the manner of the excellence of the opening (bara'at al-istihlal), and to make clear that he, peace be upon him, despite his lofty rank and great sanctity, has been held lawful (istahallu) in this sacred city, and they confronted him with what is not good, and they intended what they did not attain. From Shurahbil: "They forbid themselves to kill game therein and to cut down a tree therein, yet they consider lawful the expulsion of you and your killing."

Or it is to console him, peace be upon him, with the promise of its conquest, in the sense: "And you will be a resident of it in the future," as in the words of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die﴾. You will do with it what you wish of killing and captivity. And so it was, when Allah made Makkah lawful for him, peace be upon him, and granted him its conquest, and it was not conquered for anyone before him nor made lawful for anyone else. So he, peace be upon him, made lawful therein what he willed and forbade what he willed: he killed Ibn Khatal while he was clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah, and Maqis ibn Subabah, and others besides them, and he forbade the house of Abu Sufyan. Then he said: "Indeed Allah made Makkah sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth. It is sacred until the Hour is established. It was not made lawful for anyone before me, and it will not be made lawful for anyone after me, and it was made lawful for me only for an hour of a day. Its trees shall not be cut, its grass shall not be uprooted, its game shall not be startled, and its lost property shall not be taken except by one who announces it." Al-Abbas said: "O Messenger of Allah, except the idhkhir (a fragrant grass), for it is for our smiths and our graves and our houses." So he, peace be upon him, said: "Except the idhkhir."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 90, verse 3:**

﴿And by the begetter and what he begot﴾ is in apposition (ʿaṭf) to ﴿this city﴾. What is meant by the begetter is Abraham, and by ﴿what he begot﴾ is Ishmael and the Prophet, may the blessings of God be upon them all, as indicated by the thing joined to them, for it is the sanctuary of Abraham, the place of growth of Ishmael, and the birthplace of the Messenger of God, peace be upon them. The expression of them by "what" (mā) rather than "who" (man) is for magnification and exaltation, like the indefiniteness of "a begetter." Mentioning them under the title of begetting is a suggestive preparation (tarshīḥ) for the content of the answer, implying that it is realized in both states of being a parent and being a child. (p-161)

It has been said: Adam, peace be upon him, and his offspring. This is more suitable to the content of the answer in that it encompasses all. However, the magnification derived from the word mā requires that a generalization (taghlīb) be considered in it. It has also been said: every begetter and what he begot.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 90, verse 4:

﴿Indeed, We created man in kabad.﴾ That is: in toil and hardship, for he continually suffers the various kinds of hardships from the time the soul is breathed into him until it is extracted, and what lies beyond that. It is said: "kabida al-rajul kabdan" when his liver (kabid) was afflicted, and its origin is: "kabadahu" when it struck his liver. Then the usage was broadened so that it came to be used for every fatigue and hardship, and from it the word al-mukabadah (enduring hardship) is derived. As it was said, "kabatahu" with the meaning of "ahlakahu" (destroyed him). And this is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he was enduring from the disbelievers of Quraysh.

The pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Does he think﴾, refers to some of those who opposed the one (ﷺ) and inflicted upon him what he endured, such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and his likes. It is said that it refers to Abu al-Ashudd ibn Kaladah al-Jumahi. He was extremely strong and was deceived by his strength. A leather hide from 'Ukaz would be spread out for him, and he would stand on it and say: "Whoever removes me from it, for him is such-and-such." Then ten men would pull him, and he would be torn into pieces, yet his feet would not slip. That is: does this strong, insolent one, who oppressed the believers, think ﴿that no one will have power over him﴾?

The word ﴿أنْ﴾ (an) is the lightened form of ﴿أنَّ﴾ (anna), and its noun, which is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), is omitted. The meaning is: does he think that no one will be able to take revenge on him?

﴿He says, "I have squandered wealth in abundance."﴾ He means the great quantity of what he spent on what the people of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance) used to call makarim (noble deeds), and called ma'ali (exalted deeds) and mafakhir (glories).
﴿Does he think that no one has seen him?﴾ [He thinks this] when he was spending, and that He, exalted is He, does not call him to account for it nor reward him for it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 90, verse 8:

﴿Did We not make for him two eyes?﴾ He sees with them.

Qur'an 90:9 — "And a tongue and two lips."

﴿And a tongue﴾ by which he expresses what is in his inner self.

﴿And two lips﴾ with which he covers his mouth, and by which he is aided in speech, eating, drinking, and other things.
ﷻ "And We guided him to the two paths" (al-najdayn): that is, the paths of good and evil; or, the two breasts. The root meaning of najd is a raised, elevated place.

Translation:

﴿But he has not attempted the steep path.﴾ That is: he did not give thanks for those magnificent blessings through righteous deeds, and He expressed them by "the steep path" (al-'aqabah), which is the road through a mountain, because of the difficulty of traversing it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 90, verse 12:

The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And what will make you know what the steep path is?﴾ That is: what made you know what the breaking-through of the steep path (iqtiham al-'aqaba) is, in order to further emphasize its greatness and that it holds an exalted station with Allah the Exalted.
﴿Freeing a neck﴾ — i.e., it is the emancipation of a slave.
﴿Or feeding on a day of severe hunger﴾, that is, a day of famine.
﴿Orphan with near kinship﴾, i.e., kinship.

﴿Or a needy person in misery﴾ — that is, in destitution. Since the meaning of "the steep path" (iqtiham al-'aqabah) here is these matters, it is good to have "la" (not) before the past tense verb, for it hardly ever occurs except repeated; the meaning being: "so he did not free a neck, nor did he feed an orphan or a needy person." The words al-maskhaba (hunger), al-maqraba (kinship), and al-matraba (destitution) are all on the pattern mafa'alah, from sagiba (he went hungry) and qaruba min al-nasab (was near in kinship) and tariba (he became destitute). It is also read as "fakka raqabatan" or "at'ama," in substitution for "iqtahama."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 90, verse 17:

﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause negated by "lā" (not). The particle "thumma" (then) indicates the remoteness of the rank of faith and the elevation of its station, since all righteous deeds are conditioned upon it.

﴿And enjoined one another to patience﴾ It is coordinated with "āmanū" (they believed), meaning: some of them enjoined others to be patient in obedience to God.

﴿And enjoined one another to compassion﴾ That is, to show mercy to His servants, or to the things that necessitate His mercy of good deeds.

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring back to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who"), in view of its being characterized by what occurs in its relative clause. The sense of distance in the demonstrative, together with the recent mention of the referent, indicates the great distance of their rank in nobility and excellence. That is: those who are described by the sublime attributes mentioned.

﴿the companions of the right hand﴾ That is: of the right (اليَمِين) or of blessing (اليُمْن).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 90, verse 19:

﴿And those who disbelieve in Our signs﴾: in what We have set up as a proof of the truth, from a Book and a clear argument, or in the Qur'an.

﴿They are the companions of the left hand﴾: that is, the left (al-shimal), or the misfortune (al-shu'm).

﴿Over them is a fire sealed shut﴾, meaning closed over, from *āṣadtu al-bāb* (I shut the door), when I closed it and locked it. It is also read as *"mūṣadah"* without a hamza, from *awṣadtuhu*.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Balad, Allah the Exalted will grant him security from His anger on the Day of Resurrection."
